newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb rulers take tough stance as protests continue.
newsitem.headline: Serb rulers take tough stance as protests continue.

text.p: Serbia's ruling Socialists are taking a tough stand against demonstrations as the opposition keeps up protests after winning its main goal of overturning election fraud.

In a strongly worded statement by Parliament speaker Dragan Tomic and in editorials appearing on Thursday in state-backed newspapers, President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialists said it was time for protests to stop now that election victories of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition are being restored.

"From the moment... when a positive solution for Zajedno was absolutely certain, it became certain that the promise made by (Zajedno co-leader) Vuk Draskovic... that the demonstrations would stop as soon as parliament recognises the election results would amount to nothing," Politika Ekspres said.
The newspaper's editorial, read during the evening news programme of state-run Serbian television on Wednesday, said Zajedno leaders were "eager for street power".

It said the protests, which began three months ago over election fraud, would be kept up to "liberate the media" -- but warned that "only those who think the same as coalition Zajedno can appear in the 'free' media".
Zajedno and their student allies, who fought the election fraud by mounting daily demonstrations for 12 weeks, said they would not let up the pressure for the government to make additional reforms.
The students' demands include the sacking of the Belgrade University rector and a student co-rector while one of Zajedno's demands is for greater access to strictly-controlled state media.

Earlier, Parliament speaker Tomic said citizens were "frightened" by the marches and they should stop now that Parliament had passed a law reinstating Zajedno victories in 14 cities annulled for "irregularities" after November elections.
"These marches of groups of citizens in parts of the city appeared horrific," Tomic, one of the hard-liners in President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist party, told Radio Belgrade.
"It is not only a matter of disturbing citizens but of a kind of violence. Those shouts and cries must frighten any peaceful citizens."

Tomic accused the Zajedno leaders, who were invited to several European countries over the past three months to signal Western displeasure with Milosevic, of having sold out Serbia by asking the West to re-impose sanctions.
"That is unheard of. Never will you find an example that a true patriot, for the sake of political passion, will seek to have his country put in a chain and in a dungeon," he said.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno co-leader, was dismissive of the parliament speaker's comments saying, "He has said what we already know -- that Tomic is afraid of his own people.

"Every spontaneous gathering of people defending their rights appears to him as a threat...This shows how estranged from the people the authorities are and why these protests must take place at all," Djindjic told reporters.

Some 15,000 students marched in Belgrade at mid-day on Wednesday and thousands of Zajedno supporters watched in the evening as a red boat, about 1.5 m (five-feet) long, was launched in the Danube River.
Demonstrators chanted "Out, Slobo (Milosevic), out" and sang "And Now Addio" as the boat symbolically carrying the Socialists "out to sea" was set adrift, to an accompanying display of fireworks.
"Communism has finally gone down the river and there is no communism in Serbia as of tonight," Djindjic said.
The West has cautioned Milosevic against using force on peaceful demonstrators and to open dialogue with his rivals, notably on the issues of access to the media.
In return Zajedno leaders are reported to have promised the West they would stop testing Milosevic's patience on the streets once their victories are reinstated.
